unit_metadata.thesis_one_sentence: Heidegger's SS 1924 lecture course is methodologically philological in a rigorous academic sense — its conceptual centeredness, text-centered Greek reading, and rejection of presuppositionless philosophy together constitute a hermeneutic-phenomenological philology that exceeds the horizon of classical philology and finds its prefiguration in Aristotle's Rhetoric as the hermeneutic of concrete Dasein.

hierarchical_outline.heading: [Opening — no heading]
argumentative_moves: Frames the surprise: SS 1924 'Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy' is announced as a course on philology, not on philosophy or its history (book p. 65, citing note 1 = GA 18 4, 333).

Two relevant points of intellectual history (book pp. 65-67): (1) Heidegger's prior multi-year project of laying bare the primordial concern of Aristotelian thinking via Destruktion of philosophical-theological systemicity (Aquinas, Thomism, Catholic theology), with Bultmann as a closer ally than Natorp/Hartmann in releasing the authentic kerygma from distorting Greek philosophical conceptuality.

(2) Marburg 1920s philological cooperation: a strictly philological cooperation between philosophy, theology, and philology departments; numerous reading circles attested by Gadamer's published recollection (note 3 = Philosophische Lehrjahre 14ff).

Werner Jaeger's 1923 Aristoteles attempted a reconstruction of Aristotelian philosophy as a whole emerging from piecemeal philological work; placed philosophers in the position of needing to argue philologically as well as philosophically.

Gadamer's testimony (note 4, Grondin biography 139): Jaeger's book brought home to Gadamer 'as a philosopher, the need for a thorough training in philology... Philosophical and philological questions cannot be posed independently of each other.'

Sets up the chapter's two-part structure: §I will examine whether Heidegger's claim to do philology is confirmed; §II will pursue the strong hypothetical claim that 'if philology were to denote passion for the knowledge of that which has been expressed and of its self-expression [Leidenschaft der Erkenntnis des Ausgesprochenen und des Sichaussprechens], then his aim and his procedure would be purely philological' (book p. 66, citing GA 18 4, 333).

Notes the lecture course's parallel occasional usage of hermeneutics, signaling that SS 1924 belongs to Heidegger's recasting of Husserlian reflexive phenomenology as hermeneutic phenomenology; the second part will inquire into philology's relation to Aristotle's treatment of rhetoric, addressed in the lectures under the heading 'hermeneutic of Dasein' (book p. 67).

hierarchical_outline.heading: I. HEIDEGGER AS CLASSICAL PHILOLOGIST
argumentative_moves: Heidegger relies almost exclusively on the texts of Aristotle themselves, with the history of Aristotelianism 'so to speak, bracketed' (book p. 67); reference to Porphyry, Boethius, Kant, Hegel only to show that scholastic logic degenerated logos as horismos as logos ousias into mere thought-technique recoverable only by return to Aristotle (GA 18 9f, 15f, 335f).

On the affects (Wirkungsgeschichte): the Stoics, church fathers, Aquinas, Luther are not read for augmentation of understanding but to show that Aristotle's pathē-doctrine exerts tremendous influence and is the necessary basis for those discussions (GA 18 177f).

Two apparent exceptions — Themistius/Simplicius and Nietzsche — are introduced 'not so much as philosophers but as philologists.' Themistius/Simplicius commentaries on Physics III.1-3 used (GA 18 319, 369, 376, 381, 386, 394). Nietzsche's 'History of Greek Eloquence' lecture in Philologica vol. 2 likely studied (book p. 68).

The decisive feature: 'apart from the texts of Aristotle himself no philosophical authorities whatsoever are admitted as interpretive aids, whereas at least a few philological authorities are' (book p. 68).

Werner Jaeger's central role: Jaeger's book is the only text Heidegger recommends to students as secondary reading — but with the warning that Jaeger addresses precisely what Heidegger does not (personality, system, development; note 5 = GA 18 5, 333f).

Switching of labels noticed: 'Jaeger, the classical philologist, gives us philosophy; Heidegger, the philosopher, gives us philology' (book p. 68). Tempting admonition: not to look too rashly for a philosophical system in Aristotle but to be content with — even proceed more philologically than — Jaeger.

Heidegger accepts certain isolated conclusions of Jaeger on literary character, relative chronology, authenticity of Aristotelian corpus writings (GA 18 4f, 37, 107, 239, 323), but disapproves of Jaeger's developmental-historical reconstruction project: 'It is my conviction that this effort is altogether hopeless' (GA 18 299).

Other philologists used: Hermann Diels (source for exoterikoi logoi as nonscientific discourse founded on prevailing opinions; etymology of entelecheia, GA 18 107, 296, 367f); Ludwig Spengel (conjecture of pre-Aristotelian authorship for Rhetorica ad Alexandrum); Hermann Bonitz (Index Aristotelicus on use of ousia, GA 18 113f, 345). For lexicology, etymology, authenticity, Heidegger places himself under recognized scholars.

Aristotle as sui ipsius interpres (Luther's sola scriptura applied to Aristotle): Heidegger's approach is concept-centered and to that end text-centered/reading-centered/hearing-centered — 'the understanding of some fundamental concepts of Aristotelian philosophy' to be gained 'by way of the study of the text of the Aristotelian treatises' (GA 18 3, 5).

Two principles of textual interpretation Heidegger asserts in passing (book p. 69): (1) As reader, the interpreter must show that interpretation 'stands in the text itself' and is not 'fabricated,' that it 'has its ground' in the text (GA 18 216, 237). (2) As listener, the interpreter must go beyond the text to what is genuinely said and meant, since interpretation 'is nothing else than emphasizing what is not there' (GA 18 66).

Both principles play equal part in Heidegger's interpretation of zoē as being-in-the-world (note 7 = GA 18 234f, where Heidegger admits the interpretation might initially be held to be 'read into' Aristotle and defends its validity from De partibus animalium).

Translation practice: Heidegger does not cite from existing German translations but gives his own translation/paraphrase, often formulated at the podium. His rough, imprecise practice makes evident that 'the character of translation is in principle experimental, provisional, and always incomplete' (book p. 70). Whenever he notices a mistake — or has it pointed out by his audience 'astonishingly strong in Greek' — he takes deliberate pains to set things aright (GA 18 222, 226f).

Range of texts: Heidegger occupies a middle ground between fickle leaping and immanent preoccupation with a single text. Guided by the question of Bodenständigkeit der Begrifflichkeit (rootedness/autochthony of conceptuality), he attends to interrelated text segments before following thread to next.

Concept-centeredness in detail: Heidegger pays close attention to prephilosophical/nonphilosophical (natural) language usage of the Greeks. The reflection on metapherein (transference) explicitly raised by Aristotle himself — 'first and primordial' meaning addressing of something transferred to a new way of addressing a thing, the borrowed meaning seen as such (GA 18 83). Example: soma as 'body' refined — corporeality not as Stoffllichkeit (stuffiness) or Materialität (materiality), but as 'strange obtrusiveness' of a being detected in to son soma, su, soma meaning 'slave' or 'prisoner' (GA 18 28, 347).

Translation philosophy: when fundamental concepts tend to remain untranslated (in both Heidegger's German translations of Aristotle and in his interpretive remarks), the German translations either get more precise meanings or are explicitly rejected and replaced by something that comes nearer to Heidegger's preferred meaning.

Hekaston example (GA 18 32): 'This is not each [jedes] or even single and individual. Hekaston means what in each case obtains [Jeweiliges] insofar as I linger with it and thereby see it from a certain distance.' Available translations 'block the path that leads to understanding insofar as they cling to thinking with an excessive familiarity.'

Other examples: telos — not Ziel/Zweck but Ende in the sense of completion (note 11 = GA 18 39); ousia — not Wesen but Dasein in the sense of being available (GA 18 25, 40); aisthesis — not Empfindung but Vernehmen the world in the sense of having-it-there (GA 18 52); energeia — not Wirklichkeit but Im-Werke-Sein in the sense of a distinctive 'how' of being (ausgezeichneten Wie des Seins).

Etymological discussions employed: the Aristotelian neologism entelecheia from enteles and echein — Heidegger rejects 'Possession of completeness' [Besitz der Vollkommenheit] as not conveying the ontologically fundamental meaning, substituting 'holding-itself-in-completion' [Sich-im-Fertigsein-Halten] (note 13 = GA 18 368; cf. 296, 302, 303 for further etymology with -de suffix and kategoria).

Verdict (book p. 72): Heidegger may be said to engage in philology in a rigorously academic sense — enlists multiple philologists, applies genuinely philological methods, places original text and concepts at center. BUT not entirely a classical philologist: fails to take into account research literature extensively; does not consistently/self-sufficiently apply specialized current methods. POSITIVELY: his conceptual discussions order concepts via the guiding question of autochthony of conceptuality into a systematic whole that EXCEEDS the horizon of classical philology.

hierarchical_outline.heading: II. PHILOLOGY, HERMENEUTIC PHENOMENOLOGY, AND RHETORIC
argumentative_moves: Pivot question (book p. 72): What is remarkable is that Heidegger explicitly rejects the title of philosophy in favor of philology even for this region that exceeds the horizon of classical philology.
Differentiation from Jaeger plays a role; Heidegger gives further indications.

Critical aside to colleagues (GA 18 169f): 'it would perhaps be a good idea if philosophers would resolve to consider what it actually means to speak to others' — a critique of philosophical teaching's lack of self-conscious reflection on Sachcharakter (substantive character) of speaking, listeners, discourse.

Polemical reformulation (note 14 = GA 18 6, citing the manuscript at GA 18 334): 'philosophy today is in better shape [than philology], provided that it maintains the fundamental presupposition that things could not be better' [es sei alles in bester Ordnung]. I.e., philosophy maintains the illusory presupposition that it stands under no presuppositions; regards itself as presuppositionless and letztbegründend (having an ultimate foundation).

Definition of philology against this: an attempt to conduct research and teaching while confronting the claim made by presuppositions involved in such practices, and seeking to understand fundamental conditions of one's own discourse.

Six presuppositions of the philological intent of the lecture (note 15 = GA 18 5, 333f): #1 = Aristotle alone whose discourse is relevant — philology not just a method but a fundamental matter of concern in its own right; #2 = philologist must not regard himself as so far advanced he has nothing more to learn; #3-#5 = particular status of the discourse called for; #6 = philologist must attribute to historical past in general, to which Aristotle belongs, a saying-power that reaches the philologist himself.

Heidegger's concept of philology entails: researcher/teacher recognizes that on his own he can never achieve adequate reflection on what is said; remains dependent on impulse from tradition; essential impulse comes from Aristotle.

Conceptual discourse is not merely medium for definition/communication but the SUBSTANCE of all scientific research; this scientific research is not external incidental circumstance of life but a possibility of existence for which human beings must choose and decide.
In contrast to religious existence: philology — possibility in which human existence takes up a position with regard to its own interpretation centered solely on itself.
Hence: philology is the existentially-ontologically grounded directive of scientific research (book p. 74).

Heidegger's lecture directed to students in every department, challenging them to take up study of Aristotle 'to really grasp it and to pursue it in such a way that the activity of conceptual research comes to life' (note 16 = GA 18 14, 339).

'Not in the sense of a scientific propaedeutic that must be completed before science proper can begin, but rather in the sense of a task that, in connection with the objects of study, is always to be undertaken anew' (book p. 74; cf. note 17 = GA 18 339: 'one stands in the matter').

Closer reading of philology = 'passion for the knowledge of that which has been expressed and of its self-expression' (note 18 = GA 18 333; manuscript wording differs slightly): philo-logy as philia of logos, a 'love of speaking.' Heidegger's 'love'-as-'passion for knowledge' privileges THEORETICAL conception over PRACTICAL.
Yet theoretical cognition does not stand in contrast to practical exercise of speech by its indifference toward its object; like practical speech, it remains carried along by 'passion.'

Aristotle's notion of pathos = Heidegger's 'attunement' (Befindlichkeit) — designated as the historical impulse for Heidegger's existential-ontological thematization of attunement of Dasein (note quoted: GA 18 4, 120, 168). Just as theory in Aristotle is a state of being composed (Gefasstsein) against pathos of fear (specifically: that what is constantly there [das Immerseiende] could perhaps cease to be — GA 18 289f), so existential ontology takes science as a possibility of existence grasped by Dasein, attuned, disposed by moods.
For the philologist: the question of cognition of speech (Erkennen des Sprechens) is a matter of philologist's attuned and comprehending being-in-the-world (befindlich-verstehendes In-der-Welt-sein).

Heidegger's definition of philology unfolds speech as the duality 'of that which has been expressed and of its self-expression' [des Ausgesprochenen und des Sichaussprechens] — indicating the structural multiplicity of the Aristotelian concept of LOGOS. To wit: (1) Legein — 'speaking' in sense of accessing/addressing/showing forth; speaking with and to others; ability to listen to such speaking and self-expression (Sich-selbst-Aussprechen / Sichaussprechen). (2) Legomenon — 'the spoken,' 'that which has been expressed' (Ausgesprochenes) in sense of an answer, what is shown forth by the being addressed (von dem angesprochenen Seienden). (3) Legein-and-at-the-same-time-legomenon — 'speaking' and 'that which has been expressed' in sense of something that just pops into one's head and comes out, something that is no longer one's own and has become generally available public property (note quoted: GA 18 17, 19f, 104f, 123f, 212, 216f, 276f, 304, 341, 358).

Task of philological knowledge: separate the logos into its multiple structural moments. Philology aims at conceptual speaking in scientific research/teaching — situating it in structural whole of human speaking, made transparent in its genesis from that speaking.

Philology shows what makes up conceptuality of concepts as distinct from nonconceptual speaking; how this conceptuality is rooted in speaking as fundamental attunement of being of human beings, and thereby in Dasein itself as being of human beings.
Investigates everyday self-expression with others concerning whatever contributes to end of one's concerns — where average understanding (Dasein as anyone, als Man) finds expression (GA 18 55f, 63f).

But because logos in third sense (idle chatter) comes to prominence and obscures genuine meaning: possibility of the concept first appears in possibility one has of disregarding everyday concerns and appropriating genuine meaning in original way as countermove against idle chatter (GA 18 217, 276f).

Concept can also and immediately sink back into idle chatter and betray what was originally appropriated (note 19), so philology must on conceptual level delimit authentically conceptual speaking from inauthentic.

Question of relation to broader hermeneutic phenomenology project (Heidegger pursued since War Emergency Semester 1919; finally drafted in Sein und Zeit 1927): Heidegger mentions phenomenology only sparingly in Aristotle lectures, only in form of allusion to what is Aristotelian in phenomenology and what is phenomenological in Aristotle.
One place criticism of phenomenology: Heidegger asserts superiority of Aristotelian insight over claim of phenomenology (GA 18 199, 237, 254).

Talk of hermeneutics on the rise: in preference to logic and ontology, considered more appropriate title for thematization of Dasein; in sense of interpretation of concrete Dasein, designated as topic of Aristotle's RHETORIC (note 20 = GA 18 110 and 337; cf. 270, 351, 380f, 403).

Hermeneutics present in fact: Heidegger distinguishes three moments of conceptuality in Dasein — concrete fundamental experience, guiding claim, prevailing intelligibility — accounted for by fore-having, fore-sight, fore-grasping as three moments of interpretedness of Dasein.

Concrete fundamental experience: the experience of a being in its primary appearance forming basis of further concept formation, presents object in advance — possible by means of fore-having, in which attuned Dasein already has there before itself the world and beings. Guiding claim (addressing of beings in accord with sense of being): possible by fore-seeing, in which understanding Dasein in its dealings with world looks toward particular sense of being. Prevailing intelligibility (conceptual explication that suffices to provide acceptable standard of knowledge/evidence): possible by fore-grasping, in which Dasein grasps determinations of beings in dominating way and renders them distinguishable (note quoted: GA 18 13f, 270f, 338f, 354f).

As hermeneutical, phenomenology seeks access to things themselves from starting point of interpretedness of Dasein — by explicit appropriation of fore-having, fore-seeing, fore-grasping it throws into relief along with interpretedness governing in historical Dasein the distortions through which Dasein conceals things.

To extent that current prevalence of form of interpretedness with distortions inherent in it is carried by logos that as everyday idle talk (or even inauthentic conceptual talk) governs all interpretations of Dasein in ever greater distance from things — to such an extent PHILOLOGY (in sense of thematization of authentic conceptual speech that takes shape as countermovement against such idle talk) is disclosed as a NECESSARY ELEMENT of hermeneutic phenomenology: it is the element with which hermeneutic phenomenology takes into account the leading function of speech in dominance of interpretedness of Dasein.

Pivot to RHETORIC (book p. 77): Some of what Heidegger says about Aristotle's Rhetoric makes clear he sees this conception of hermeneutic-phenomenological philology PREFIGURED there: the Rhetoric attests to a primordial viewing of speech, the phenomena of which are surveyed and distinguished in terms of basic possibilities Dasein has of speaking-with-one-another (Miteinandersprechen) — the result being an interpretation of concrete Dasein as being-with-one-another (Miteinandersein) (note 22 = GA 18 110, 113, 117, 139, 358, 276 — citing the entire Rhetoric (61), and key formula 'The Rhetoric is nothing else than the interpretation of concrete Dasein, the hermeneutic of Dasein itself' from GA 18 110).

Two respects in which philology cannot be equated with rhetoric: (1) Philology — even if passionate — remains a theoretical cognition of speech, whereas rhetoric as treated by Aristotle represents the practical possibility of seeing what speaks for the subject matter for whoever is resolved to convince others of something (GA 18 114f). Only insofar as Aristotle's Rhetoric maintains a theoretical character throughout its general reflection on fundamental conditions/possibilities of discourse — only to this extent can the Rhetoric be regarded as a predecessor to Heideggerian philology.

(2) Philology has to do primarily with conceptual speech of scientific research and teaching, whereas rhetoric deals primarily with everyday speaking-with-one-another that Dasein directs toward regulation of its everyday being-with-one-another (book p. 78). Philology MUST disclose idle talk as negative impulse for development of conceptual speech, but exceeds scope of rhetoric in direction of what Aristotle himself delimits from rhetoric as DIALECTIC (note 23 = GA 18 127f on paradeigma/enthymema vs. epagoge/syllogismos as parallel forms of speech dealt with by rhetoric and dialectic respectively).

Closing formula (note quoted: GA 18 7): 'Dialektikē has, to be sure, its seriousness (the same that has been lost by every philosophy that has become sophistry). But this is only the seriousness of an attempt at seeing what could ultimately be meant (by the concepts). In this sense we are dealing with philosophy.'

hierarchical_outline.heading: NOTES (23 numbered)
argumentative_moves: Note 1: Defines GA 18 as Grundbegriffe der aristotelischen Philosophie: Marburger Vorlesung Sommersemester 1924, Gesamtausgabe vol. 18, ed. Mark Michalski (Frankfurt: Klostermann, 2002), 4, 333. ESTABLISHES THE 'HENCEFORTH ALL PAGE REFERENCES NOT OTHERWISE SPECIFIED ARE TO THIS TEXT' CONVENTION.
Note 2: Translator's note on German parentheticals being his insertions (Findling).
Note 3: Gadamer's Philosophische Lehrjahre (1977), 14ff — Marburg reading circles testimony.
Note 4: Quoted in Grondin biography of Gadamer (1999), 139 — Jaeger inspiring Gadamer's philological turn.
Note 5: GA 18 4, 333; cf. Werner Jaeger, Aristoteles: Grundlegung einer Geschichte seiner Entwicklung (Berlin: Weidman, 1923).
Note 6: Sechs Briefe an Martin Heidegger aus der Marburger Zeit (1999), 14f; Gadamer review of Jaeger 'Werner Jaeger, Aristoteles' in Gesammelte Werke 5: Griechische Philosophie I (1985), 286f.
Note 7: Heidegger admits zoe-as-being-in-the-world interpretation might initially be held to be 'read into' Aristotle, defends it via De partibus animalium (GA 18 234f).
Note 8: Examples — Metaphysics 5.16 on teleion (GA 18 83f), Rhetoric 2.5 on phobos (GA 18 249f), and Physics 3.1-3 with three approaches to definition of kinēsis (GA 18 287f, 316, 323f).

Note 9: Consideration of agathon in NE 1.1-6 interrupted by consideration of teleion in Met 5.16 precisely where teleion shows itself as criterion for agathon in sense of telos di hauto (GA 18 80f). Of different text groups, predominant ones broadly ethical/ontological, but Topics (152f) and natural science De partibus animalium (208f) also receive look.
Note 10: Self-citation: Michalski, 'Terminologische Neubildungen beim frühen Heidegger,' Heidegger Studies 18 (2002): 181-191.

Note 11: Heidegger on telos translation (GA 18 39): 'The translation of telos by purpose or goal obviously has some basis... The question is whether these translations are primary, and whether one is permitted, at this level of the investigation into being, to mix up primary and derivative meanings' (GA 18 82). 'Purpose and goal are founded on telos as end as the primordial meaning' (GA 18 85).
Note 12: 'If our expression reality [Wirklichkeit] were not so well worn, it would be an excellent translation' (GA 18 70) — over-familiarity of word as decisive criterion for rejecting translation.
Note 13: GA 18 368; cf. 296, 302, 303 for further etymology with -de suffix and kategoria.

Note 14: GA 18 6; cf. manuscript formulation: 'Philosophy, by contrast, especially today, does not need [the presuppositions], because it maintains the fundamental presupposition that things could not be better' (GA 18 334).

Note 17: 'The precondition of being-able-to-be-attentive is that one stands in the matter. Hence it is not the case that you can just spend a semester speculating about concepts while saying to yourself: Well, first I have to know what philology is, then I can begin. Such a person will never reach the beginning, because he will never get to know what philology is' (GA 18 339).
Note 18: GA 18 333. This is the wording in the manuscript. In the text taken from student notes (GA 18 4) the ending words 'and of self-expression' are missing.

Note 19: GA 18 276f: 'This [that the logos bears within itself as idle chatter the possibility of distortion (Verstellen)] refers not only to the everyday... but directly concerns in a much sharper degree the interpretation of Dasein that would make research and philosophy into explicit tasks of Dasein. It can happen that certain logoi once expressed, precisely in times when research is young and lively, take on such a prominence that for a long time they make inaccessible the very beings they intend.'
Note 20: GA 18 110 and 337. On use of adjective 'hermeneutic,' cf. 270, 351, 380f, 403.
Note 21: GA 18 358, 276 quoted: 'The being of this dominance lies in logos.' 'The dominance of the interpretedness has the logos. The logos is the authentic bearer of interpretedness.'

Note 22: GA 18 110, 113, 117, 139 quoted with the central formula 'The Rhetoric is nothing else than the interpretation of concrete Dasein, the hermeneutic of Dasein itself' (GA 18 110), and 'Today, we have only a primitive impression [Vorstellung] of speech... The concrete instance of the primordiality of seeing is the entire Rhetoric' (GA 18 61).
Note 23: GA 18 127f — paradeigma/enthymema vs. epagoge/syllogismos as parallel forms of speech dealt with by rhetoric and dialectic respectively.

key_concepts.name: Philology (Heidegger's existential-ontological sense)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Per Heidegger's hypothetical formula: 'passion for the knowledge of that which has been expressed and of its self-expression' [Leidenschaft der Erkenntnis des Ausgesprochenen und des Sichaussprechens] (GA 18 4, 333). Philology is the existentially-ontologically grounded directive of scientific research; not propaedeutic to science but a task always to be undertaken anew. It is the philia of logos understood as theoretical cognition that nonetheless remains 'carried along by passion.'

key_concepts.name: Hermeneutic phenomenology
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's recasting of Husserl's reflexive phenomenology, pursued since War Emergency Semester 1919 and systematically drafted in Sein und Zeit 1927. As hermeneutical, phenomenology seeks access to things themselves from starting point of the interpretedness of Dasein, throwing into relief — by explicit appropriation of fore-having, fore-seeing, fore-grasping — the distortions through which Dasein conceals things.

key_concepts.name: Passion for knowledge of the expressed and of self-expression
key_concepts.german_form: Leidenschaft der Erkenntnis des Ausgesprochenen und des Sichaussprechens
key_concepts.english_form: passion for the knowledge of that which has been expressed and of its self-expression
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's hypothetical formulation of philology (GA 18 4, 333). The German technical formula that, were philology so denoted, would make Heidegger's aim and procedure 'purely philological.' The duality des Ausgesprochenen / des Sichaussprechens indicates the structural multiplicity of the Aristotelian concept of logos. Note: the manuscript (GA 18 333) has the full formula; the student-notes text (GA 18 4) drops the trailing 'and of self-expression' (per note 18).

key_concepts.name: Destruktion (destructuring)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's pre-1924 multi-year project of laying bare the primordial concern of Aristotelian thinking by destructuring philosophical-theological systemicity and conceptuality layered upon it through the philosophical tradition (Aquinas, Thomism, Catholic theology).

key_concepts.name: Logos (structural multiplicity)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger reads the Aristotelian concept of logos as having three structural moments: (1) Legein — speaking-as-accessing/addressing/showing-forth, including listening and self-expression (Sichaussprechen); (2) Legomenon — the spoken, that which has been expressed (Ausgesprochenes), shown forth by the being addressed (von dem angesprochenen Seienden); (3) Legein-and-at-the-same-time-legomenon — what just pops into one's head and comes out, no longer one's own, generally available public property [= idle talk territory].

key_concepts.name: Rhetoric as hermeneutic of Dasein
key_concepts.english_form: Aristotle's Rhetoric as the hermeneutic of concrete Dasein
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Per GA 18 110: 'The Rhetoric is nothing else than the interpretation of concrete Dasein, the hermeneutic of Dasein itself.' The Rhetoric attests to a primordial viewing of speech; phenomena surveyed and distinguished in terms of basic possibilities Dasein has of speaking-with-one-another (Miteinandersprechen) — yielding interpretation of concrete Dasein as being-with-one-another (Miteinandersein). Prefigures Heidegger's hermeneutic-phenomenological philology.

key_concepts.name: Idle chatter / idle talk
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Logos in its third sense — what just pops into one's head and comes out, generally available public property. Comes to prominence and obscures genuine meaning. Philology must on conceptual level delimit authentically conceptual speaking from inauthentic, since the concept can sink back into idle chatter and betray what was originally appropriated.

key_concepts.name: Average understanding / Anyone
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Mode in which Dasein comports itself in everyday self-expression with others, where average understanding finds expression. Philology investigates what contributes to end of one's concerns through this everyday self-expression (GA 18 55f, 63f).

key_concepts.name: Attunement (Heidegger's translation of pathos)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger translates Aristotle's pathos as Befindlichkeit (attunement) in the lecture course — designated as the historical impulse for Heidegger's existential-ontological thematization of attunement of Dasein (GA 18 4, 120, 168). Just as Aristotelian theory is a state of being composed (Gefasstsein) against pathos of fear (specifically: that das Immerseiende could one day cease to be — GA 18 289f), so existential ontology grasps science as a possibility of existence attuned by moods.

key_concepts.name: Attuned and comprehending being-in-the-world
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: The mode of being from which the philologist's question of the cognition of speech (Erkennen des Sprechens) is posed.

key_concepts.name: Three moments of conceptuality / fore-structure of interpretedness
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: The three moments of conceptuality Heidegger distinguishes in Dasein — concrete fundamental experience, guiding claim, prevailing intelligibility — are accounted for by fore-having, fore-sight, fore-grasping as the three moments of the interpretedness of Dasein. Concrete fundamental experience presents object in advance via fore-having; guiding claim addresses beings via fore-seeing; prevailing intelligibility renders distinguishable via fore-grasping. Hermeneutic phenomenology accesses things by explicit appropriation of these three.

key_concepts.name: Autochthony of conceptuality / rootedness of conceptuality
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's guiding question — the autochthony of conceptuality — orders his concept-discussions and his text-handling. Pays close attention to prephilosophical/nonphilosophical (natural) language usage of the Greeks since technical terms are rarely neologisms but typically formed out of common/familiar words through discrete measures of semantic shift.

key_concepts.name: Metapherein (transference)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: The event of meaning-transference explicitly raised by Aristotle himself — meaning borrowed from 'first and primordial' addressing and transferred to a new way of addressing a thing; the borrowed meaning seen as such (GA 18 83). Heidegger takes this event into account whenever it lends itself to investigation of 'first and primordial' meaning.

key_concepts.name: sui ipsius interpres (Aristotle interpreting himself)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Luther's principle of sola scriptura applied to Aristotle by Heidegger: the texts of Aristotle alone whose interpretation matters; reference to Porphyry/Boethius/Kant/Hegel only to show degeneration; Stoics/church fathers/Aquinas/Luther only to show Wirkungsgeschichte; even Themistius/Simplicius/Nietzsche introduced as philologists not philosophers.

key_concepts.name: Translation as experimental, provisional, incomplete
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's rough/imprecise translation practice makes evident that 'the character of translation is in principle experimental, provisional, and always incomplete.' Rules out the erroneous notion that a translation could ever replace the Greek text and render superfluous the necessity of reading and attending to the original. Heidegger does not cite from German translations but gives his own translation/paraphrase, often formulated at the podium (GA 18 222, 226f).

key_concepts.name: Being-at-work (Heidegger's translation of energeia)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger rejects standard German Wirklichkeit ('reality'/'actuality') as too well-worn (GA 18 70) and substitutes 'Im-Werke-Sein' — being-at-work in the sense of a distinctive 'how' (ausgezeichneten Wie) of being. Note 12: over-familiarity (Abgegriffenheit) of a word is decisive criterion for rejecting a translation.

key_concepts.name: Holding-itself-in-completion (Heidegger's translation of entelecheia)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Aristotelian neologism from enteles + echein. Heidegger rejects 'Possession of completeness' (Besitz der Vollkommenheit) as failing to convey the ontologically fundamental meaning, substituting 'holding-itself-in-completion' (Sich-im-Fertigsein-Halten) — note 13 = GA 18 368.

key_concepts.name: Hekaston (each-time-this / what in each case obtains)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger refuses 'each' (jedes) or 'single/individual' as standard renderings. 'Hekaston means what in each case obtains [Jeweiliges] insofar as I linger with it and thereby see it from a certain distance' (GA 18 32). Available translations 'block the path that leads to understanding insofar as they cling to thinking with an excessive familiarity.'

key_concepts.name: zoē as being-in-the-world
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotelian zoē as being-in-the-world — flagged by Heidegger himself (note 7 = GA 18 234f) as one that might initially be held to be 'read into' Aristotle, but which he defends from De partibus animalium. Both reader-principle and listener-principle play equal role.

key_concepts.name: Topology of conceptuality (philology vs. rhetoric vs. dialectic)
key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's tri-partition: rhetoric deals primarily with everyday speaking-with-one-another (regulating everyday being-with-one-another); philology deals primarily with conceptual speech of scientific research and teaching (which discloses idle talk as negative impulse); dialectic (which Aristotle delimits from rhetoric) is the seriousness lost by every philosophy that becomes sophistry (GA 18 7, 127f).

main_positions.claim: Heidegger's SS 1924 lecture course can legitimately be said to engage in philology in a rigorously academic sense — measured by enlistment of multiple philologists (Jaeger, Diels, Spengel, Bonitz, Themistius, Simplicius, Nietzsche), application of genuinely philological methods (lexicology, etymology, authenticity criticism), and centering of the original Greek text and its concepts.
premises: Heidegger announces SS 1924 as a course on philology, not on philosophy or the history of philosophy (GA 18 4, 333).
Heidegger admits no philosophical authorities as interpretive aids apart from Aristotle himself (Aristotle as sui ipsius interpres / sola scriptura).
Heidegger does admit philological authorities (Jaeger as recommended secondary reading; Diels, Spengel, Bonitz for lexicology/authenticity).
Heidegger's text-centered, concept-centered, listening-centered procedure is genuinely philological (GA 18 3, 5, 333).
Translation practice (rough, podium-formulated, experimental) and respect for critical apparatus confirm philological orientation.
targets: The view that Heidegger's procedure is freely philosophical-systematic appropriation of Aristotle.
The view that Heidegger arrogantly ignored or misused existing German Aristotle translations (book p. 70: 'such accusations... quite simply fail to do him justice').

main_positions.claim: Heidegger is NOT entirely a classical philologist: he fails to take the research literature into account extensively and does not consistently/self-sufficiently apply the specialized philological methods then current; positively, his conceptual discussions order concepts via the guiding question of the autochthony of conceptuality (Bodenständigkeit der Begrifflichkeit) into a systematic whole that EXCEEDS the horizon of classical philology.
premises: Heidegger disapproves of Jaeger's developmental-historical reconstruction project: 'It is my conviction that this effort is altogether hopeless' (GA 18 299).
Critical apparatus is consulted (translations rejected/inserted based on corresponding texts) but the goal is not philological-historical reconstruction.

Heidegger's translation practice substitutes ontologically motivated terms (Im-Werke-Sein for energeia, Sich-im-Fertigsein-Halten for entelecheia, Jeweiliges for hekaston, Vernehmen for aisthesis) — not standard philological renderings.
His guiding question is the autochthony of conceptuality — a systematic-philosophical question, not a strictly philological one.
targets: Reduction of Heidegger to classical philologist tout court.
Equation of Heidegger's procedure with Jaeger's developmental Aristotle scholarship.

main_positions.claim: Heidegger's strong hypothetical formulation in SS 1924 — 'If philology were to denote passion for the knowledge of that which has been expressed and of its self-expression [Leidenschaft der Erkenntnis des Ausgesprochenen und des Sichaussprechens], then his aim and his procedure would be purely philological' (GA 18 4, 333) — is not a vague concept-borrowing but a determinate redefinition of philology as the existentially-ontologically grounded directive of scientific research.
premises: Heidegger replaces 'philosophy' with 'philology' in his self-description, even for the region exceeding classical philology's horizon (book p. 72).
Philosophy maintains the illusory presupposition that it is presuppositionless and letztbegründend (note 14 = GA 18 6, 334).
Philology, by contrast, conducts research while confronting the claim made by presuppositions involved.

Six presuppositions enumerated by Heidegger (GA 18 5, 333f) define philology positively: Aristotle's unique relevance; philologist as continuing learner; conceptual discourse as substance of all scientific research; scientific research as a possibility of existence Dasein chooses; Aristotle's saying-power reaching the philologist.
targets: Heidegger's philosophical colleagues' presuppositionless self-conception (Heidegger's critique of Husserl's reflexive phenomenology indirectly).
Conventional academic philology that lacks existential-ontological grounding.

main_positions.claim: Philology as Heidegger develops it is the philia of logos understood as theoretical cognition that nonetheless remains 'carried along by passion' — preserving the Aristotelian structure of pathos/Befindlichkeit (translated by Heidegger as attunement) in the philologist's mode of attuned and comprehending being-in-the-world (befindlich-verstehendes In-der-Welt-sein).
premises: Philology = philia of logos, 'love of speaking,' where 'love' is explicated as 'passion for knowledge' (GA 18 333).
Heidegger privileges theoretical conception over practical one as the meaning of philology's love.
Yet theoretical cognition does not stand against practical exercise of speech but, like it, remains carried by 'passion.'
Aristotle's pathos = Heidegger's Befindlichkeit, designated as historical impulse for existential-ontological thematization of attunement of Dasein (GA 18 4, 120, 168).

Aristotelian theory as Gefasstsein against pathos of fear (specifically: das Immerseiende ceasing to be — GA 18 289f) parallels existential ontology's grasp of science as Dasein's possibility, attuned by moods.
targets: Pure-theory or pure-practice readings of philology that miss the pathic-attunement-bound structure.

main_positions.claim: Philology in Heidegger's sense is a NECESSARY ELEMENT of hermeneutic phenomenology — the element with which hermeneutic phenomenology takes into account the leading function of speech in the dominance of the interpretedness of Dasein — because logos governs all interpretations of Dasein, as everyday idle talk or even inauthentic conceptual talk, in ever greater distance from things.
premises: Hermeneutic phenomenology accesses things from starting point of interpretedness of Dasein, throwing into relief — by appropriation of fore-having, fore-seeing, fore-grasping — the distortions through which Dasein conceals things (GA 18 13f, 270f, 338f, 354f).
Logos as everyday idle talk / inauthentic conceptual talk carries the current prevalence of distorted interpretedness.
Philology is the thematization of authentic conceptual speech as countermovement against idle talk (GA 18 217, 276f).
Therefore philology is what hermeneutic phenomenology requires to take account of speech's leading function in dominance of interpretedness.
targets: Reading hermeneutic phenomenology without its philological moment.
Reading SS 1924 as either pure phenomenology or pure philology rather than philology as a moment of hermeneuticizing phenomenology.

main_positions.claim: Aristotle's Rhetoric prefigures Heidegger's hermeneutic-phenomenological philology because the Rhetoric attests to a primordial viewing of speech, surveying phenomena in terms of basic possibilities Dasein has of speaking-with-one-another (Miteinandersprechen), thereby producing an interpretation of concrete Dasein as being-with-one-another (Miteinandersein).
premises: GA 18 110: 'The Rhetoric is nothing else than the interpretation of concrete Dasein, the hermeneutic of Dasein itself.'
GA 18 61: 'The concrete instance of the primordiality of seeing is the entire Rhetoric.'
GA 18 117: 'In the Rhetoric we have before us something that deals with speech as a fundamental mode of being understood as the being-together of human beings themselves.'

GA 18 139: 'We can take the Rhetoric as a concrete guiding thread insofar as it is nothing else than the interpretation of Dasein with respect to the basic possibilities of speaking with one another.'
targets: Reading Aristotle's Rhetoric as merely a practical-pedagogical handbook for orators.

main_positions.claim: Heideggerian philology cannot, however, be equated with rhetoric: (1) philology even if passionate remains theoretical cognition of speech, whereas Aristotle's rhetoric represents the practical possibility of seeing what speaks for the subject matter for whoever is resolved to convince others; (2) philology has to do primarily with conceptual speech of scientific research/teaching, whereas rhetoric deals primarily with everyday speaking-with-one-another that regulates everyday being-with-one-another. Philology exceeds rhetoric's scope in the direction of what Aristotle himself delimits from rhetoric as DIALECTIC.
premises: Aristotle's Rhetoric maintains a theoretical character throughout its general reflection on fundamental conditions/possibilities of discourse (GA 18 114f) — only to this extent can it be regarded as predecessor to Heideggerian philology.
Philology must disclose idle talk as negative impulse for development of conceptual speech but exceeds rhetoric's everyday-regulation scope.

Heidegger explains how he proposes to deal philologically with philosophy precisely in connection with dialectic: 'Dialektikē has, to be sure, its seriousness (the same that has been lost by every philosophy that has become sophistry). But this is only the seriousness of an attempt at seeing what could ultimately be meant (by the concepts). In this sense we are dealing with philosophy' (GA 18 7).
Note 23 = GA 18 127f on paradeigma/enthymema (rhetoric) vs. epagoge/syllogismos (dialectic) as parallel forms of speech.
targets: Identification of Heideggerian philology with rhetoric simpliciter (which would miss the dialectical-philosophical seriousness).

main_positions.claim: Heidegger's SS 1924 procedure constitutes a methodologically authoritative model that constrains how all subsequent readers of GA 18 — and by extension of the genesis of Sein und Zeit — may legitimately interpret Heidegger's appropriation of Aristotle: any reading must register both the rigorously philological-textual operations and their existential-ontological exceeding of classical philology.
premises: Michalski's status as editor of GA 18 (Klostermann 2002) gives this framing scholarly weight (he has read the manuscript wording; cf. note 18 distinguishing manuscript from student-notes wording).
The SS 1924 lectures are continuous with the broader project (1919 War Emergency Semester onward) systematically drafted in Sein und Zeit 1927.
Mentions of phenomenology in the lectures occur 'only sparingly... only in the form of an allusion to what is Aristotelian in phenomenology and what is phenomenological in Aristotle' (book p. 76).
Hermeneutics' rise replaces logic and ontology as title for thematization of Dasein.
targets: Methodologically uncritical readings that flatten Heidegger's philological operations into a pure systematic philosophy.
Methodologically uncritical readings that flatten Heidegger's existential-ontological exceeding into pure classical philology.
Implicitly: Kisiel's primarily political reading of GA 18, which underweights the philological constraint.

Rhetorica ad Alexandrum (Spengel conjecture)
Categories — kategoria etymology (GA 18 303)
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed (sui ipsius interpres) — Aristotle is the only philosophical authority Heidegger admits as interpretive aid; the historical past has saying-power that reaches the philologist himself.

interlocutors.name: Werner Jaeger
citations: Aristoteles: Grundlegung einer Geschichte seiner Entwicklung (Berlin: Weidman, 1923) — note 5
Gadamer review in Gesammelte Werke 5: Griechische Philosophie I (1985), 286f — note 6
interlocutors.relationship: contrasted (label-switching: 'Jaeger, the classical philologist, gives us philosophy; Heidegger, the philosopher, gives us philology'). Heidegger accepts Jaeger's isolated conclusions on literary character/chronology/authenticity (GA 18 4f, 37, 107, 239, 323) but rejects Jaeger's developmental-historical reconstruction as 'altogether hopeless' (GA 18 299).

interlocutors.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
citations: Philosophische Lehrjahre (Frankfurt: Klostermann, 1977), 14ff — note 3 (Marburg reading circles)
Sechs Briefe an Martin Heidegger aus der Marburger Zeit (1999), 14f — note 6
'Werner Jaeger, Aristoteles' (review) in Gesammelte Werke 5 (1985), 286f — note 6

Vita-testimony quoted in Grondin's biography (1999), 139 — note 4: Jaeger 'brought home to Gadamer as a philosopher the need for a thorough training in philology... Philosophical and philological questions cannot be posed independently of each other.'
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed — Gadamer's testimony is the chief external witness Michalski enlists for the Marburg philological cooperation context and for the inseparability of philosophical and philological questions.

interlocutors.name: Rudolf Bultmann
citations: Implied in book p. 65 — 'striving in corresponding fashion to release the authentic kerygma of the New Testament from the distorting conceptuality of Greek philosophy.'
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed — Heidegger's Destruktion finds 'more solidarity' with Bultmann's parallel project on the New Testament than with Natorp/Hartmann.

interlocutors.name: Paul Natorp
citations: Named at book p. 65.
interlocutors.relationship: contrasted — Natorp's systematic philosophical disposition is what Heidegger has less solidarity with than Bultmann's philological-theological project.

interlocutors.name: Nicolai Hartmann
citations: Named at book p. 65.
interlocutors.relationship: contrasted — same as Natorp: Heidegger's philological-Destruktion project is at greater distance from Hartmann's systematic disposition than from Bultmann's parallel work.

interlocutors.name: Thomas Aquinas / Thomism
citations: Named at book p. 65 within 'philosophical-theological systemicity and conceptuality... layered upon such thinking.'
interlocutors.relationship: critiqued — the philosophical-theological tradition Heidegger destructures in his pre-1924 project.

interlocutors.name: Catholic theology
citations: Named at book p. 65.
interlocutors.relationship: critiqued — the conceptuality 'layered upon' Aristotelian thinking that Destruktion lays bare.

interlocutors.name: Hermann Diels
citations: GA 18 107, 296, 367f — entelecheia etymology and exoterikoi logoi as nonscientific discourse founded on prevailing opinions (note in book p. 69).
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed — Heidegger places himself under Diels for lexicology, etymology, authenticity in 'craft of classical philology.'

interlocutors.name: Ludwig Spengel
citations: Conjecture of pre-Aristotelian authorship for Rhetorica ad Alexandrum (book p. 69).
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed — Heidegger uses Spengel's authenticity-criticism conclusion.

interlocutors.name: Hermann Bonitz
citations: Index Aristotelicus on use of ousia (GA 18 113f, 345).
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed — Heidegger consults the Index Aristotelicus for ousia usage.

interlocutors.name: Themistius / Simplicius
interlocutors.role: Late-classical commentators read 'as philologists not as philosophers'
citations: Aristotle's Physics III.1-3 commentaries (GA 18 319, 369, 376, 381, 386, 394) — book p. 67.
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed — Heidegger uses the commentaries' philological data on Physics III but does not treat them as philosophical authorities.

interlocutors.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
interlocutors.role: Apparent exception introduced as philologist not philosopher
citations: Aperçu that Greek is the 'most speakable of all languages' (book p. 68); 'In the final analysis he must have known what it is to be Greek' [GA 18 109].
'History of Greek Eloquence' lecture in Philologica vol. 2 (likely studied — book p. 68).
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed — Nietzsche enlisted as natural classical philologist, not as philosopher.

interlocutors.name: Porphyry / Boethius / Kant / Hegel
interlocutors.role: Scholastic/post-scholastic philosophical tradition cited only to show degeneration
citations: GA 18 9f, 15f, 335f — on logos as horismos as logos ousias degenerated into mere thought-technique (book p. 67).
interlocutors.relationship: critiqued — these philosophical authorities not admitted as interpretive aids; mentioned only as data of Wirkungsgeschichte.

interlocutors.name: Stoics / church fathers
citations: GA 18 177f — on Aristotle's pathē-doctrine as basis for Stoic/patristic affect-discussions (book p. 67).
interlocutors.relationship: critiqued (as interpretive aids) / illustrative (as Wirkungsgeschichte) — they show Aristotle's tremendous influence but do not augment understanding of Aristotle.

interlocutors.name: Martin Luther
interlocutors.role: Source of sui ipsius interpres principle (sola scriptura applied to Aristotle)
citations: Implied at book p. 69: 'Luther's principle of sola scriptura seems to find application here: Aristotle sui ipsius interpres.'
Also named at book p. 67 as Wirkungsgeschichte of pathē-doctrine.
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed (the principle) / critiqued (as interpretive aid for Aristotle) — the principle is appropriated; Luther himself is not admitted as Aristotle-interpreter.

interlocutors.name: Edmund Husserl
interlocutors.role: Reflexive phenomenology that Heidegger recasts as hermeneutic phenomenology
citations: Implied at book p. 67: Heidegger 'recasts the reflexive phenomenology of Husserl as a hermeneutic phenomenology.'

Implied criticism (book p. 76): 'one place there is even a kind of criticism of phenomenology, when Heidegger asserts the superiority of an Aristotelian insight over a claim of phenomenology' (GA 18 199, 237, 254).
interlocutors.relationship: critiqued / refined — Heidegger recasts Husserl's reflexive phenomenology rather than rejecting it; presupposes the Husserlian project as the framework his philological project hermeneuticizes.

interlocutors.name: Jean Grondin
interlocutors.role: Biographer of Gadamer (source for Gadamer's vita-testimony on Jaeger)
citations: Hans-Georg Gadamer: Eine Biographie (Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 1999), 139 — note 4.
interlocutors.relationship: borrowed — Grondin's biography is the source for Gadamer's archival testimony on Jaeger's impact.

tensions_and_open_questions.tension: Philology is rigorous philology AND not entirely classical philology — Michalski's verdict (book p. 72) is calibrated against two opposing absolute readings: (a) Heidegger as merely a freely systematic philosopher using texts illustratively; (b) Heidegger as classical philologist tout court. Both are rejected, but the positive characterization — 'a systematic whole that EXCEEDS the horizon of classical philology' — leaves the precise relation of Heidegger's procedure to classical philology partly open.

The 'passion for knowledge' formula privileges THEORETICAL over PRACTICAL conception of philology, yet theoretical cognition 'remains carried along by passion' as practical exercise of speech does (book p. 75). This is the textually faithful position but it places considerable weight on the precise sense in which 'theoretical' here is sustained by Befindlichkeit (attunement) — i.e., by the Aristotelian pathos — rather than being purified of it. The boundary between theoretical-as-attuned philology and Aristotelian-rhetorical practice (which is precisely about everyday speaking-with-one-another) remains a matter of degree.

tensions_and_open_questions.tension: The Aristotle/philosophical-tradition asymmetry: Aristotle alone is admitted as philosophical authority (sui ipsius interpres), but the historical past in general is given 'saying-power that reaches the philologist himself' (per the sixth presupposition, GA 18 5, 333f). How is the singular authority of Aristotle reconciled with the saying-power of the (presumably wider) historical past? Michalski preserves the textual claim but does not address the apparent restriction.

VT7 (Phase 0): Phenomenology versus philology. Michalski makes the strong claim that Heidegger 'explicitly rejects the title of philosophy in favor of philology even for this region that exceeds the horizon of classical philology' (book p. 72) — yet philology is also a 'necessary element of hermeneutic phenomenology' (book p. 77). The titular question of the essay receives a synthetic rather than a dichotomous answer: phenomenology is hermeneuticized, hermeneutic phenomenology requires the philological moment, and philology in this enlarged sense IS the existentially-ontologically grounded directive of scientific research.

Michalski's philological framing of GA 18 contrasts with Kisiel's protopolitical reading (HR-06-KISIEL). Where Kisiel reads the SS 1924 lectures as the genesis text of a 'rhetorical protopolitics' with Arendtian afterlife, Michalski reads them as a methodologically authoritative philology that exceeds classical philology in the direction of dialectic and philosophy. Both readings cite GA 18 110 (the Rhetoric-as-hermeneutic formula) but draw different categorial consequences. This is the most direct intra-volume methodological contrast: how is GA 18 to be read — as a philological exercise, or as a political-historical genesis text?

tensions_and_open_questions.tension: Michalski's reading of philology as theoretical cognition of speech (carried by passion but not practical-resolute) is in tension with Hyde's reading of the call of conscience as 'an ontological and emotional form of epideictic rhetoric' (HR-04-HYDE). Hyde's epideictic-as-call extends rhetoric into the existential register that Michalski reserves for philology-beyond-rhetoric. The point of contact is the role of Befindlichkeit/pathos: Michalski makes attunement the philologist's mode (befindlich-verstehendes In-der-Welt-sein, book p. 75); Hyde makes attuned address the orator's epideictic register. Michalski's identification of pathos as Befindlichkeit (Heidegger's translation, GA 18 4, 120, 168) and as the philologist's mode of attuned-comprehending being-in-the-world supports Gross's pathos-as-substrate genealogy (Intro IV) by anchoring the pathos/Befindlichkeit equation in the SS 1924 lectures themselves. Jaeger as the foil: 'Jaeger, the classical philologist, gives us philosophy; Heidegger, the philosopher, gives us philology.' The label-switching contrast frames the entire §I argument that Heidegger's procedure is genuinely philological in a non-Jaegerian sense.

Gadamer's testimony (Philosophische Lehrjahre 14ff; Grondin biography 139): philosophical and philological questions cannot be posed independently of each other. This supports Michalski's Marburg-philological-cooperation framing of SS 1924.

Heidegger's hermeneutic phenomenology is the recasting of Husserl's reflexive phenomenology (book p. 67); GA 18 199, 237, 254 even contains a criticism of phenomenology (book p. 76). The Husserlian project is presupposed-and-recast.
